title: The Yerkes-Dodson Dilemma
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart applies the Yerkes-Dodson curve — the psychological principle that performance peaks under moderate, not minimal or maximal, pressure — to the daily experience of teaching. He argues that staying atop the curve yields maximized effectiveness, enjoyment, and a sense of meaning in the work, but that most teachers default toward one of two failure modes: burnout from excessive perfectionism and internal or external pressure, or disengagement from boredom, emotional injury, or not knowing how to combine deep care with sustainable practice. He offers a simple two-step diagnostic — figure out where you are on the curve, then apply the proper remedy — with concrete suggestions for each side, from observing colleagues or taking on a new challenge when under-pressured, to walking or granting yourself permission to be good enough when over-pressured. He closes with a wry caution against turning stress-management itself into another source of stress.
points: Frames teacher burnout and disengagement as two symmetric failure modes off the same Yerkes-Dodson curve, rather than as unrelated problems.
Prescribes a concrete two-step process — locate yourself on the curve, then apply the matched remedy — rather than a single one-size-fits-all fix for stress.
Points to a specific example, committing to one pop-up debate per week, as how he personally re-engaged himself when under-challenged.
Names the meta-trap of stressing about managing your stress, a reminder that self-improvement efforts can themselves become another pressure source.
quotes: So much of effective teaching — and good living — comes down to how well you manage to stay atop the Yerkes-Dodson Curve.
On one side of the curve, you're burnt out and stretched thin. It's easy to get here because the work we do is important, which means there's tons of internal and external pressure sources.
But on the other side of the curve, you find yourself unchallenged, bored, and apathetic. You're disengaged; you're going through the motions.

If you're on the under-pressured side, you can do things like observe a colleague, read (and apply!) a new PD book, ask someone to sit in on your lessons, or set a challenge for yourself for the next month of your teaching.
And in all of it, don't get stressed about managing your stress. The last thing we want is to add pressure to our pressure because we feel pressure to make it perfect.
